prize_parts.citation: For foundational contributions to the theory of nominal rigidities and monetary policy rules, which established the New Keynesian framework for analysing monetary policy.

statement.case_for: The B014 case rests on originality, breadth and durability, and the attribution problem can be handled by a discovery-focused citation. Calvo's time-dependent pricing and Taylor's staggered contracts and policy rule introduced the two mechanisms on which the framework rests. Woodford's microfounded, welfare-based synthesis turned them into a coherent theory of interest rates, prices and optimal policy. Together they changed how central banks reason about and communicate policy, and they became standard teaching and research tools over four decades. Colleagues' attribution arguments moved me from my opening trio (Woodford, Taylor, Galí) to Calvo, Taylor and Woodford. Galí's New Keynesian Phillips curve and his empirical work are important, but they build on Calvo pricing and Woodford's synthesis, so a citation about the pricing friction and the policy rule is best credited to the three who introduced them. I still hold that Rubinstein–Wolinsky (B006) is an outstanding piece of theory. My move reflects the weaker marginal case for it next to B014 in this cycle, because of its narrower reach beyond theory and the recent run of prizes in neighbouring areas of microeconomic theory. It does not reflect a lower view of its scientific merit.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Christiano, Eichenbaum and Evans (identification of monetary shocks and the medium-scale model), Galí, Gertler and Smets–Wouters all made major contributions, and a cap of three excludes people whose work made the framework empirically usable. A second reservation is that the framework did not anticipate the 2008 crisis and was stressed by the 2021–23 inflation. That may refine rather than undermine the core contribution, but the committee has not settled the matter. Third, honouring the originators of the pricing friction and the rule may be read as rewarding the older conceptual layer over the estimated DSGE layer that central banks actually run.

responses.point: Krusell proposes Calvo, Taylor and Woodford as the most distinct conceptual contributions (price-setting, contracts and rule, and synthesis). He concedes that excluding Galí, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets is a real cost, and that post-2008 and post-2021 debates may temper views of the framework.
responses.response: I largely agree and have changed my own trio to match his. Galí's New Keynesian Phillips curve follows from Calvo pricing inside the Woodford-type synthesis, so it is better seen as a development than a separate foundation. I would qualify one point. The Christiano–Eichenbaum–Evans claim is not merely derivative. It concerns identifying monetary shocks and estimating a medium-scale model, which is a different kind of contribution, and a citation limited to mechanisms and rules does not capture it. I treat this as a real cost of the three-person cap, not a resolved question.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B006 fourth with the same Rubinstein–Wolinsky pair as mine. He worries about reluctance to award game theory again after the 2005, 2007, 2012 and 2020 prizes, about overlap with search-and-matching recognition (2010), and about whether Wolinsky's share justifies inclusion.
responses.response: Part of this persuades me. Those prizes covered conflict and cooperation, mechanism design, stable allocations and auctions. Non-cooperative alternating-offers bargaining was not among them, and Rubinstein–Wolinsky is distinct from the Diamond–Mortensen–Pissarides search framework because it derives bargaining outcomes from decentralised trade. On Wolinsky, I think the 1985 paper makes him a genuine co-originator rather than a add-on. But I work in neighbouring areas (matching, auctions, mechanism design) and may overrate theory that I read closely. I therefore give the saturation concern real weight and keep B006 only as an alternative.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B014 second with Woodford, Galí and Taylor. He flags a possible tension with the narrative that the framework failed to anticipate 2008 and 2021–22, and a possible saturation of macro-monetary work (Lucas, Sargent and Sims, Kydland and Prescott, Bernanke). He ranks B047 (Melitz, Helpman) first.
responses.response: I accept the performance concern but would not call the field saturated. The earlier prizes rewarded rational expectations, time consistency, VAR methods and banking-crisis analysis. None rewarded the nominal-rigidity pricing mechanism, the policy-rule literature or the normative synthesis that these three supplied. On B047 I agree Melitz's 2003 contribution is clear and the framework is mature. I rank it below B014 because of the Krugman (2008) overlap, which blurs its novelty, and because of the unresolved credit for Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, who are not on the ballot. I do not think attribution is cleaner for B047 than for B014 once these are counted.

responses.point: Strömberg ranks B003 first with Moore, Kiyotaki and Gertler. He argues that collateral-constraint amplification is a foundational macro-finance mechanism, and that the 2022 prize makes this a related rather than duplicative recognition.
responses.response: I agree that Kiyotaki–Moore is a foundational and well-attributed mechanism, and I keep B003 as an alternative. I disagree on Gertler. Most colleagues restrict the proposal to Kiyotaki and Moore, and Gertler's financial-accelerator work was done with a laureate (Bernanke, 2022). Gertler also appears in B014. My opening trio for B003 included him, but I would now propose Kiyotaki and Moore if B003 became the lead case. I also think the 2022 overlap is real. It makes the committee's choice between B003 and B014 a judgement about novelty, not simply about merit.

uncertainties: Whether Galí, Christiano and Eichenbaum, or Gertler have a stronger claim than Calvo, Taylor or Woodford for a citation centred on the policy framework, and whether the committee prefers a narrower citation (pricing friction or policy rule) to the broader New Keynesian framework.
How much weight to give the framework's performance in the post-2021 inflation and the heterogeneous-agent critique when judging maturity.

Whether the recent prizes in microeconomic theory should lower the weight on B006 relative to its scientific merit, and whether Binmore's contribution should count against the Rubinstein–Wolinsky pair.
How strongly the 2022 prize overlap should count against B003, and whether Gertler belongs in a B003 award.
I have not independently verified priority and attribution claims from outside the supplied evidence.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile for Calvo, Taylor or Woodford. The profile lists no co-authorship or institutional link with them or with the other B014 names. My field is microeconomic theory and market design, which is adjacent to B006 (Rubinstein, Wolinsky). I note that proximity as a possible familiarity bias, not a recusal-level connection. My SSE affiliation with committee colleagues is not a link to any candidate.
